questions.stem: In May 1916, after an attack on the ferry Sussex, Germany gave the 'Sussex pledge'. Why did its end in February 1917 bring the United States close to war?
options: Germany had promised not to sink merchant ships without warning, and broke that promise
Germany had promised to pay for the Lusitania, and then refused all compensation
Germany had promised to stay out of Mexico, and then invaded the state of Texas
Germany had promised to buy American wheat, and then cancelled all its contracts
questions.explanation: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917, gambling it could starve Britain before America made a difference. With American ships sunk and the Zimmermann Telegram published, Congress declared war on 6 April 1917.

questions.stem: The Zimmermann Telegram, published in the United States in March 1917, revealed that Germany had:
options: offered to end submarine attacks if the US stopped lending money to Britain and France
asked Japan to attack the Philippines and Hawaii if the US entered the war
promised to give Canada to the United States in return for American neutrality
proposed an alliance with Mexico, offering it lost land in the US south-west
questions.explanation: Intercepted and decoded by British intelligence, the telegram offered Mexico Texas, New Mexico and Arizona if it joined a war against the US. Its publication turned many Americans, especially in the West, against Germany.

questions.stem: When he asked Congress to declare war in April 1917, Woodrow Wilson justified American entry mainly as:
options: a war to win colonies in Africa and the Pacific from the German Empire
a response to a direct German invasion of United States territory
a duty owed to Britain under a secret alliance signed before 1914
a fight to make the world safe for democracy, not for territory
questions.explanation: Wilson framed the war in idealistic terms, and later set out his Fourteen Points. The United States joined as an 'associated power' rather than a formal ally of Britain and France, and sought no territory.

questions.stem: The Committee on Public Information, headed by George Creel from 1917, was set up to:
options: build public support for the war through posters, films and speakers
investigate war profiteering by businesses supplying the army in France
censor all letters sent home by American soldiers serving overseas
plan the peace terms Wilson would present at the Paris conference
questions.explanation: The CPI used 'Four Minute Men' speakers, posters and films to sell the war. Its propaganda also encouraged suspicion of German Americans and dissenters, contributing to wartime intolerance.

questions.stem: Under the Espionage Act (1917) and the Sedition Act (1918), the socialist leader Eugene Debs was:
options: elected to Congress on an anti-war platform in 1918
deported to Russia with other foreign-born radicals
appointed to run the War Industries Board in 1918
jailed for a speech opposing the war and the draft
questions.explanation: Debs was sentenced to ten years for an anti-war speech in 1918 and ran for president from prison in 1920. In Schenck v. United States (1919) the Supreme Court upheld such laws, ruling that speech creating a 'clear and present danger' could be restricted.

questions.stem: Which development best shows that the First World War changed American society as well as foreign policy?
options: Wilson presented his Fourteen Points as a basis for a just peace
Hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved north for war jobs
The US Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles and the League of Nations
American troops of the AEF helped halt the German offensives of 1918
questions.explanation: Wartime labour shortages drew large numbers of southern Black workers to northern cities in the Great Migration, reshaping urban America and politics. The other options concern foreign and military policy.

questions.stem: The 'Red Summer' of 1919 refers to:
options: the arrest of thousands of suspected radicals in the Palmer Raids
the spread of influenza through army camps at the end of the war
attacks by white mobs on African Americans in cities such as Chicago
a wave of communist uprisings that briefly took control of American cities
questions.explanation: Tensions over jobs and housing, and returning Black veterans' demands for rights, led to riots in some two dozen cities in 1919, the worst in Chicago. The Palmer Raids of 1919-20 targeted radicals and are a separate event.

questions.stem: Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association, which drew mass support in the early 1920s, promoted:
options: integration through lawsuits against segregated schools
alliance with white trade unions to win higher wages
nonviolent sit-ins against segregated public places
Black pride, economic independence and return to Africa
questions.explanation: Garvey's movement attracted hundreds of thousands with its message of racial pride and businesses such as the Black Star Line. He was convicted of mail fraud and deported in 1927. Legal action against segregation was the NAACP's strategy.

questions.stem: The Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s was:
options: a Democratic Party campaign to win Black votes in northern cities
a flowering of Black literature, music and art centred in New York
a building program that replaced Harlem's slums with public housing
a religious revival led by fundamentalist preachers in the southern states
questions.explanation: Writers such as Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston, and musicians such as Duke Ellington, expressed a new Black cultural confidence. It drew on the Great Migration that had made Harlem a centre of Black life.

questions.stem: The Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC), created in 1933, provided:
options: pensions for retired workers over 65 funded by payroll taxes
insurance for bank deposits up to a fixed amount per account
work for young jobless men in forestry, parks and flood control
loans to farmers to buy land and machinery at low interest rates
questions.explanation: The CCC housed young men in camps, paying them to plant trees and build parks, with most wages sent home to families. Pensions came with the Social Security Act of 1935 and deposit insurance with the FDIC.

questions.stem: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 tried to raise farm incomes by:
options: buying all farm surpluses and exporting them to Europe at a profit
lowering tariffs so that American farmers could sell more overseas
fixing a maximum price that consumers would pay for food in shops
paying farmers to reduce production so that crop prices would rise
questions.explanation: The AAA paid farmers to plant less and even to destroy crops and livestock, controversial while people went hungry. Landowners often evicted sharecroppers, many of them African American, from land taken out of production.

questions.stem: Which law of 1935, often called labour's 'Magna Carta', guaranteed workers' right to join unions and bargain collectively?
options: the Fair Labor Standards Act, setting minimum wages
the Taft-Hartley Act, regulating union activity
the Emergency Banking Act, reforming the banks
the National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act)
questions.explanation: The Wagner Act created the National Labor Relations Board to protect union organising, and union membership grew rapidly. The Fair Labor Standards Act came in 1938, and Taft-Hartley (1947) restricted unions after the war.

questions.stem: The Works Progress Administration (WPA), created in 1935 as part of the 'Second New Deal', is significant because it:
options: paid farmers to leave the Dust Bowl and move to California
employed millions of people on public works and arts projects
ended the Depression by balancing the federal budget each year
nationalised the railways and the largest steel companies
questions.explanation: The WPA built roads, schools and airports and also employed writers, artists and musicians. It became the largest New Deal employer, though it never reached all the unemployed.

questions.stem: In 1937 Roosevelt proposed adding up to six new justices to the Supreme Court. Why is this 'court-packing' plan often seen as a political mistake?
options: It was seen as an attack on the separation of powers and split his own party
It forced the Court to strike down the Social Security Act and the Wagner Act
It required a constitutional amendment, which most states refused to ratify
It made Roosevelt lose the 1940 election to the Republican candidate
questions.explanation: Even many Democrats opposed the plan, which failed in Congress. Ironically the Court began upholding New Deal laws in 1937, but the fight, with the 1937-38 recession, weakened Roosevelt's reform momentum. He won the 1940 election.

questions.stem: Senator Huey Long of Louisiana criticised the New Deal in the mid-1930s by arguing that:
options: it did too little, and wealth should be shared through heavy taxes on the rich
it did too much, and the government should return to balanced budgets and laissez-faire
it favoured farmers over industry, and tariffs should be cut to help manufacturers
it was too generous to the unemployed and should be replaced by private charity
questions.explanation: Long's 'Share Our Wealth' plan promised every family a guaranteed income and attracted millions of supporters before his assassination in 1935. Critics from the right, such as the American Liberty League, argued the reverse.

questions.stem: Eleanor Roosevelt is significant in the New Deal years because she:
options: led the campaign that won the vote for women in 1920
travelled widely and spoke up for the poor, women and Black Americans
ran the Tennessee Valley Authority as its first chairwoman, 1933-38
served as Secretary of Labor, the first woman in the Cabinet
questions.explanation: Eleanor Roosevelt acted as her husband's eyes and ears, wrote a newspaper column and pressed for fairer treatment of African Americans. Frances Perkins was Secretary of Labor and the first woman in a Cabinet.

questions.stem: New Left historians of the 1960s, such as Barton Bernstein, judged the New Deal mainly as:
options: a socialist revolution that destroyed American free enterprise and the market
a complete failure that made the Depression longer than it would have been
a program designed mainly to win votes in the South for the Democrats
a conservative rescue of capitalism that did little to share wealth or power
questions.explanation: Bernstein argued the New Deal saved corporate capitalism and largely left out the poorest, including many African Americans and sharecroppers. Liberal historians such as William Leuchtenburg saw it as a 'half-way revolution' that greatly expanded the government's role.

questions.stem: In a December 1940 fireside chat, Roosevelt said the United States must become the 'arsenal of democracy'. He meant that it should:
options: declare war on Germany and send an army to Europe at once to fight
stay strictly neutral and refuse to sell arms to any nation
build forts to defend the American coast from invasion
supply weapons and materials to those fighting the Axis
questions.explanation: Roosevelt argued that helping Britain was the best way to keep America out of the war. The idea led to Lend-Lease in March 1941. The United States entered the war only after Pearl Harbor.

questions.stem: In 1941 A. Philip Randolph threatened to lead a mass march on Washington. Roosevelt responded with Executive Order 8802, which:
options: abolished Jim Crow laws on interstate trains and buses across the South
banned racial discrimination in defence industries and government jobs
desegregated the armed forces and ended separate Black military units
gave federal protection to African American voters in the southern states
questions.explanation: The order created a Fair Employment Practice Committee, the first federal action on job discrimination since Reconstruction, and the march was called off. The armed forces stayed segregated until Truman's order of 1948.

questions.stem: The 'Double V' campaign launched by the African American newspaper the Pittsburgh Courier in 1942 called for:
options: victory in both Europe and the Pacific before peace talks
doubling the number of Black officers in the army and navy
voting rights for both Black men and Black women in the South
victory over fascism abroad and over racism at home
questions.explanation: The campaign linked the war against Nazi racism to the struggle against discrimination in the United States. Black membership of the NAACP grew strongly during the war, helping lay foundations for the post-war civil rights movement.

questions.stem: Executive Order 9066, signed by Roosevelt in February 1942, led to:
options: the conscription of women into the army and navy for the very first time
the rationing of petrol, rubber and sugar across the United States
the forced removal and detention of about 120,000 Japanese Americans
the internment of all German Americans living on the east coast
questions.explanation: People of Japanese ancestry on the west coast, about two-thirds of them American citizens, were sent to camps. The Supreme Court upheld the removals in Korematsu v. United States (1944). In 1988 Congress apologised and paid compensation to survivors.

questions.stem: In Korematsu v. United States (1944) the Supreme Court upheld the exclusion of Japanese Americans. Why do historians use this case to discuss civil liberties in wartime?
options: The case showed that German and Italian Americans were treated identically
The case was brought by the army to stop Japanese Americans enlisting
The Court accepted a racial classification as a military necessity
The Court struck down the internment, freeing all those held in the camps
questions.explanation: The majority deferred to the government's claims of military necessity despite little evidence of disloyalty. The decision has since been widely condemned, and in 2018 the Court stated that it had been wrong on the day it was decided.

questions.stem: How did the Second World War affect American women's employment?
options: Millions took industrial jobs, though many lost them when the war ended
Women were banned from factory work so that men could have all the jobs
Equal pay laws passed in 1942 guaranteed women the same wages as men
Few women worked, because the government relied on conscripted labour
questions.explanation: Women filled jobs in shipyards and aircraft plants, symbolised by 'Rosie the Riveter', and joined auxiliary services such as the WAC and WAVES. When servicemen returned, many lost their positions, though the share of women in paid work stayed above pre-war levels.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the economic impact of the Second World War on the United States?
options: Unemployment rose because industry switched to producing weapons
Taxes were cut sharply, and war costs were met by Allied loans
War spending ended mass unemployment and output soared
The economy shrank as factories were bombed by German aircraft
questions.explanation: Huge federal spending on war production, coordinated by the War Production Board, absorbed the unemployed. Taxes were raised and broadened, with income tax withholding from wages, and war bonds were sold to the public. Many see this as evidence for Keynesian ideas.

questions.stem: The Bracero Program, begun in 1942, was an agreement under which:
options: Mexico agreed to send troops to fight alongside the US in the Pacific
Latin American countries banned trade with Germany and Japan
Mexican workers came to the US on short contracts for farm labour
American farmers moved to Mexico to grow food for the Allied armies
questions.explanation: Wartime labour shortages led the US to recruit Mexican workers, mostly for agriculture and railways. The program lasted until 1964. Mexican Americans also faced discrimination at home, as in the Zoot Suit Riots in Los Angeles in 1943.

questions.stem: In 1943 race riots broke out in Detroit and other cities. The main cause was:
options: tension over jobs and housing as workers moved to war industries
opposition to the drafting of African Americans into the armed forces
a strike by Black workers demanding an end to the war against Japan
anger at the internment of Japanese Americans in camps in Michigan
questions.explanation: Wartime migration crowded workers into cities with poor housing, and white resistance to Black workers in factories and neighbourhoods boiled over. Federal troops were sent to Detroit, where 34 people died.

questions.stem: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, known as the GI Bill:
options: guaranteed jobs in the public service for every veteran
funded college education and home loans for veterans
conscripted all men aged 18 to 45 into the armed forces
gave veterans a cash bonus that had been promised since 1924
questions.explanation: The GI Bill sent millions of veterans to college and helped them buy homes, fuelling post-war suburban growth. Black veterans, however, often found it hard to use its benefits because of discrimination in colleges, banks and local administration.

questions.stem: The Manhattan Project was:
options: the code name for the Allied landings in Normandy
a New Deal scheme to build public housing in cities
the secret wartime program that developed the atomic bomb
Roosevelt's plan to rebuild New York's docks for the navy
questions.explanation: Scientists including J. Robert Oppenheimer worked at Los Alamos and other sites. The first bomb was tested in New Mexico in July 1945, and bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.

questions.stem: Roosevelt died in April 1945, shortly into his fourth term. His successor, Harry Truman, was:
options: a Republican senator who won a special election held after Roosevelt's death
the general who had commanded the Allied invasion of Western Europe
Vice-President, and he made the decision to use the atomic bomb on Japan
Secretary of State, chosen by Congress because the Vice-President had resigned
questions.explanation: Truman had been Vice-President for only a few months and knew little of the bomb project. Roosevelt was the only president elected four times; the Twenty-second Amendment (1951) later limited presidents to two terms.

questions.stem: Studs Terkel titled his 1984 oral history of the Second World War 'The Good War', with the phrase in quotation marks. Historians have challenged the popular image of a 'good war' mainly by pointing to:
options: the failure of American industry to produce enough weapons to supply the Allies
the refusal of most Americans to support the war after Pearl Harbor was attacked
the defeat of American forces in the Pacific in 1944 and 1945
racial discrimination, Japanese American incarceration and women's treatment
questions.explanation: The war united Americans and ended the Depression, but historians stress the injustices that sat alongside victory. The other options are inaccurate: industrial output was immense, public support was strong and the US won the Pacific war.

questions.stem: A government poster from 1943 shows smiling women building aircraft under the slogan 'We can do it'. As evidence of women's wartime experience, it is most useful for showing:
options: the number of women who worked in war industries in 1943
how the government wanted to recruit women and present war work
the wages women were paid compared with men in aircraft factories
how most women felt about leaving their jobs when the war ended
questions.explanation: Propaganda reveals official aims and ideals, not typical conditions or pay. A historian would use employment statistics, oral histories and company records to test how far the image matched reality.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the view that the period 1917-1945 saw a lasting growth in the power of the federal government?
options: The Senate rejected the League of Nations after the First World War ended
Prohibition was introduced in 1920 and then repealed in 1933 by amendment
The Supreme Court struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act in 1935
Social Security, labour laws and war agencies expanded roles that outlasted 1945
questions.explanation: New Deal programs and the war economy greatly enlarged Washington's role in welfare, labour relations, taxation and the economy, and much of this remained after the war. Prohibition's repeal and the NIRA ruling show limits or reversals, not lasting growth.
